CBIR principle (Ch.10, 10.2–10.4):
① Feature extraction (Eq. 10-1): HSV space quantized to a 72-bin (8,3,3) color histogram, L1-normalized; texture uses a Sobel gradient-orientation histogram (18 bins, magnitude-weighted).
② Similarity measures: histogram intersection Sim=Σ min(h1(i),h2(i)) (Eq. 10-2); cosine similarity (Eq. 10-3); Euclidean distance (Eq. 10-4).
③ Combined similarity: Sim=0.6×color-intersection + 0.4×texture-cosine, in [0,1].
④ Color histograms are invariant to rotation/translation/scale; mirroring and rotation only slightly perturb the histogram, so images of the same content are still retrieved correctly; synthetic distractors (grass/sky/sunset/checker) rank last due to very different color distributions.

Video retrieval principle (Ch.10, 10.5):
① Keyframe extraction: video retrieval builds on image retrieval by reducing a video to a set of representative frames (12 frames uniformly sampled here; practical systems use shot boundary detection).
② Feature indexing: each keyframe is described by "HSV color histogram + gradient-orientation texture histogram", stored with its timestamp to form the video index.
③ Retrieval localization: given a frame (or its distorted copy) as query, keyframes are ranked by combined similarity; the best match's timestamp locates the content in the video — the basic principle of "search video by image".
④ Robustness: under brightness/noise/cropping distortions the color and texture features are only mildly perturbed, so the Top-1 match should still be the keyframe the query came from.
